662.t: Advice to young musicians: study the fundamentals
662.s: She urges thorough study, written work, scales, harmony and sight reading rather than playing right away, and credits her first teacher.
662.q: Well, it takes a lot of study, I can say that. But the young people don't want to study. That's right. They want to begin playing right away. But I still like that method of catechism and written work and all those sort of things. And when you're learning music. It has paid off for me. I wouldn't…

642.t: Glenny's rule: ask someone who knows
642.s: Glenny said to ask questions of someone able to answer; Guesnon names good and weak players.
642.q: Oh, yeah. Always. No, that's what he said. He said, every man can be taught something by somebody. But just so the man is not a damn fool. That's all. He said, make sure when you go to a man to ask him concerning something that the man is able to tell you what to do. And he's right. You understand?…

5.t: Advice to young players: learn the instrument, learn to read
5.s: He advises learning to handle the instrument and to read, discusses reading versus improvising on the Morton dates, and dislikes bop's complexity.
5.q: No, I, I, I don't know. I, I think, uh, I think you should learn to read and learn, first of all, learn the instrument. You know, learn how to handle the instrument. Yeah, handle the instrument. Yeah, that, I think that's the main thing. Learn how to handle that instrument and then, then, stuff

397.t: Listening to the whole band and advice to drummer students
397.s: He explains why he listens to everything, urges students to study many drummers and piano, and distinguishes drummers who play drums from those who play music.
397.q: Well that has paid big dividends in my career. Because I’m the type of drummer that always, I do a lot of listening. And I think that in my opinion, and from my experience, listening to music it is paramount. So you should listen to a lot of music, and when you listen to music, in my case I never…

673.t: Jam sessions, playing with better players, and being fortunate
673.s: Experience with audiences and better players is the way to learn; both feel lucky to make a living in music.
673.q: Experience with an audience. Also like I’m sure with Bus it’s the same thing, I used to sit in these joints and you know, you’re playing with people all the time who are better than you are. And that’s the only way to learn it. You go, like, if you’re the best kid in the band, then you’re in…

791.s: Play as much as possible, including with better players.
791.q: Play as much as you can. Whatever opportunity you have to perform, take it. The whole idea is you can’t learn how to improvise without doing it, and hopefully every day you know. That’s how you learn how to do it and do it well. So take every opportunity you can to play and play with musicians who…

606.t: Advice to young guitarists: play what you sing
606.s: Ellis says it is vital to play what you can sing, citing Joe Pass, Wes Montgomery, Clark Terry, Oscar Peterson and Ray Brown.
606.q: You mean musically? I would tell them that it’s necessary, vital that they learn to play what they sing. You know when you’re humming along with what you’re playing you know. Joe Pass did it. Wes Montgomery did it. Clark Terry does it — all the good — Oscar does it, Ray Brown does it. Anybody who…

563.s: He advises listening to the greats, playing live with others rather than play-along records, and learning solos.
563.q: No, that’s a good one. It’s something I’ve put some thought into. I’ve had some students and occasionally have private students so it’s something I’ve thought about. I think for a young aspiring jazz trumpet player of course you’ve got to listen to some of the great records and do your homework as…

611.s: His advice is to study and know harmony; he says study never hurts and knowledge makes a player sound better.
611.q: Yeah I could say that right quick, I mean study. That’s all. Study. You know what I mean? Remember that joke about the guy in the street on Seventh Avenue and another guy asked him, “how can I get to Carnegie Hall?” He says, “practice, man, practice.”

491.t: Advice to students: humility and learning from everyone
491.s: Golson tells young musicians to treat people well, think the other person is better, keep learning, and listen, citing Jay Jay Johnson, Charlie Parker and Coltrane's Weird Blues.
491.ch: Advice, education and the evolution of jazz

409.t: Advice to young players: listen to everyone
409.s: Cootie advises youngsters to listen to all good jazz players rather than one, so they find their own voice.
409.q: Well, they're entirely different. And my advice to any youngster that's coming up, not to listen to no one individual playing. Because he will never find out his identification by listening to one individual. Listen to all jazz men, all good jazz men play. Then you will become yourself. You will…
